question.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/16)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/16}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

  

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(x/4)}^{2}}}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
